identification.summary: Femwar02 is a name given in media and threat-intelligence aggregator reporting to an apparently pro-Russian ransomware actor linked to the February 2026 ransomware attack on Sapienza University of Rome. [S2][S4][S5] Italian press (Corriere della Sera, as relayed by trade media) said the attack used the Bablock (Rorschach) ransomware and may be connected to Femwar02; the university has not confirmed this. [S2][S4] Strobes and Malpedia list no campaigns before the Sapienza incident. [S5][S6]
identification.notes: The Femwar02 link rests on press reporting and aggregator entries, not on an official attribution or a vendor technical report that I could open. [S2][S4] The official university notice does not name the ransomware strain or group. [S7] Bablock/Rorschach is a separate malware family first documented by Check Point and Group-IB in 2023 and used against victims before 2026, so the malware does not by itself identify this actor. [S8][S9]

attribution.confidence: Low. Attribution to Femwar02 and Bablock is media-reported and unconfirmed by the university or Italian authorities in the sources reviewed. [S2][S4]
attribution.basis: Corriere della Sera reportedly tied the attack to Bablock and possibly to Femwar02. [S2][S4] Aggregator and Malpedia-style entries describe the actor as pro-Russian, citing that the malware leaves Russian-language files unencrypted; I could not verify that behavior in a primary technical report. [S5][S6] No state sponsor is named in any source reviewed.

objectives: Not established. The ransom link with a 72-hour countdown reported after the Sapienza attack suggests financial extortion as at least a stated aim, though that detail is reported as alleged. [S2][S3]

targeting.notes: The only incident attributed to Femwar02 in the sources is Sapienza University of Rome, beginning 2026-02-02 per press reporting (the university's later notice dates the attack 2026-02-01). [S1][S2][S5][S7] The university later said about 400 physical and virtual servers were affected, disrupting institutional portals and the InfoStud platform, with data on affected systems encrypted. [S7] Separately, Group-IB reported that Bablock/Rorschach as a malware family hit organizations in several countries including Italy; that is family-level, not Femwar02-specific. [S9]

capabilities.summary: Reporting on the Sapienza case describes Bablock/Rorschach ransomware with hybrid encryption, partial file encryption and Group Policy propagation. [S4][S5][S6] Check Point's 2023 analysis of Rorschach found code similarities to leaked Babuk source and LockBit 2.0 (I/O completion port thread scheduling), ransom notes inspired by Yanluowang and DarkSide, and loading via DLL side-loading of a Palo Alto Cortex XDR Dump Service Tool. [S8] Check Point reported very fast encryption in controlled tests. [S8][S9] Initial access vector for Sapienza is not reported in the sources reviewed.

campaigns.name: Bablock/Rorschach malware family documented (not attributed to Femwar02)
campaigns.summary: Check Point Research described the Rorschach ransomware after a US-based victim; Group-IB first publicized it in January 2023 after an incident response at a European industrial firm, and reported victims in several countries including Italy. [S8][S9]

campaigns.name: Sapienza University of Rome ransomware attack
campaigns.summary: Sapienza went offline after a cyberattack beginning 2026-02-02, shut down its network as a precaution and reported to law enforcement and Italy's ACN. [S1][S2] Media tied the attack to Bablock and possibly Femwar02, unconfirmed by the university. [S2][S4] A 72-hour ransom countdown link was allegedly sent. [S3]

campaigns.name: Incident closure and official account
campaigns.summary: The university stated that ACN closed the incident on 2026-04-02, that about 400 servers were affected, and that restoration relied on verified backups. [S7]

diamond.adversary: Femwar02, a self-unconfirmed pro-Russian ransomware actor name; no sponsor established. [S2][S5]
diamond.capability: Bablock/Rorschach ransomware (hybrid encryption, Group Policy propagation). [S4][S5][S8]
diamond.victim: Sapienza University of Rome, with about 400 servers and student/administrative services affected. [S1][S7]
diamond.socioPolitical: Pro-Russian alignment is inferred by secondary sources from the malware's reported skipping of Russian-language files; not verified. [S5][S6]
diamond.technology: Windows domain environments with Active Directory Group Policy; physical and virtual servers. [S4][S7]

gaps: Initial access vector, dwell time and any data theft for Sapienza are not reported in sources I could open.
The BleepingComputer and Security Affairs articles could not be fetched in this environment (host unreachable); their content is known only through search summaries.
Corriere della Sera original reporting and the Strobes/Malpedia/Aviatrix entries were not opened; Aviatrix appears to state details more firmly than primary reporting supports.
Whether Femwar02 is a distinct group, a persona, or a Bablock affiliate is unknown; the Russian-file skipping claim is unverified.
No official government attribution; the official university notice does not name the strain or actor.
Ransom payment and amount not confirmed.
No infrastructure indicators or other victims identified.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Step 1-2: higher-education networks in NATO partner states are a plausible target class given the Sapienza precedent, with a Windows domain and Group Policy environment as the exploited terrain. [S4][S7] Step 3: capability is a commodity-derived ransomware (Babuk/LockBit lineage) with fast partial encryption. [S8] MLCOA: further opportunistic ransomware against European public institutions with financial extortion. MDCOA: use of the same tooling against defense-related research or logistics-supporting institutions with disruption intent. Candidate indicators: unexpected Group Policy objects pushing executables, DLL side-loading of signed security-vendor tools, rapid mass file modification on domain controllers. [S4][S8]
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track Bablock/Rorschach reporting and Italian ACN/CSIRT notices; treat Femwar02 attribution as unconfirmed. [S2][S7] Authorities: incident response in the Sapienza case ran through ACN, Polizia Postale and the data protection authority, illustrating host-nation coordination paths. [S7] Mission assurance: verified offline backups and segmented domain controllers were the recovery basis. [S7] Coordination: share indicators with host-nation CSIRTs and partner cyber units before any attribution claims are used operationally.

provenance.importedSummary: Femwar02 is a previously unknown pro-Russian ransomware threat actor that emerged in early 2026, linked to a major cyberattack on Italy's Sapienza University of Rome in February 2026, which caused a full network shutdown and operational disruptions. The group deploys Bablock (also known as Rorschach), a next-generation ransomware strain first identified in 2023 that features fast hybrid encryption (curve25519 and hc-128), partial file encryption for speed, direct system calls to evade detection, and domain-wide propagation via Group Policy on Windows Domain Controllers. Bablock shares code similarities with LockBit 2.0 but incorporates elements from other families like Babuk and DarkSide, often delivered via encrypted payloads, DLL sideloading with tools like DarkLoader, and exploits such as those in Zimbra or phishing. Notably, the malware skips encrypting files written in Russian, reinforcing its pro-Russian alignment, with no prior attributions or campaigns documented before the Sapienza incident.
